n: Jesus told a parable aimed at the temple leaders. A man planted a vineyard and equipped it fully, then rented it to tenant farmers. The setup echoes Isaiah’s “song of the vineyard,” where the vineyard is Israel.

f.g: A vat or pit where grapes were pressed.
Farmers, here tenant farmers who rented the land.

n: At harvest time the owner sent a servant to collect his share of the fruit, as the rental agreement allowed.

f.g: At harvest time.

n: The tenants seized him, beat him, and sent him away with nothing.
He sent another servant; they stoned him, wounded his head, and treated him shamefully.
He sent more servants — some beaten, some killed. The servants represent the prophets God sent to Israel over the centuries.
Last of all, the owner sent his beloved only son, thinking surely they would respect him. “Beloved son” echoes the Father’s words at Jesus’ baptism.

f.g: Respect, honor.

n: The tenants plotted: this is the heir — kill him, and the vineyard will be ours. Jesus was describing the leaders’ plot against him.
They seized him, killed him, and threw his body out of the vineyard. Jesus would die outside Jerusalem’s walls.

f.w: cast him out of the vineyard

n: What will the owner do? He will come, destroy those tenants, and give the vineyard to others. Stewardship of God’s kingdom would pass to new leaders.
Jesus quoted a psalm: the stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. The rejected Son would become the foundation of everything.

f.w: The stone which the builders rejected

f.g: The cornerstone or capstone — the most important stone in the building.

n: This reversal is the Lord’s doing, and it is wonderful to see.

f.g: Wonderful, astonishing.

n: The leaders knew the parable was about them and wanted to arrest him, but they feared the crowd, so they left.
Next they sent Pharisees and Herodians — normally rivals — to trap him with his own words.

f.g: Trap him, as a hunter snares an animal.

n: With flattery they asked: should we pay taxes to Caesar or not? Saying yes would anger Jewish nationalists; saying no would be treason against Rome.

f.w: regardest not the person of men
f.g: You don’t show favoritism or care about status.
Tax, especially the Roman poll tax.

n: Seeing through their act, Jesus asked why they were testing him and requested a denarius, the Roman coin used for the tax.

f.g: A denarius, a silver Roman coin worth about a day’s wage.

n: He asked whose image and inscription were on it. They answered: Caesar’s.

f.g: Inscription — the coin named Tiberius Caesar.

n: His brilliant answer: give Caesar what belongs to Caesar, and give God what belongs to God. The coin bears Caesar’s image; we bear God’s image — so we owe ourselves to him.

f.g: Give back, pay what is owed.

f.w: to God the things that are God's

n: Next came the Sadducees, a priestly group who accepted only the five books of Moses and denied any resurrection.

f.g: An aristocratic party tied to the temple priesthood.

n: They cited Moses’ law: if a man died childless, his brother should marry the widow to give the dead brother an heir.

f.g: Have children.

n: They made up a story: seven brothers; the first married and died childless.
The second married her and died with no children, and the third the same.
All seven married her and died childless, and finally she died too.
Their trick question: in the resurrection, whose wife will she be? They meant to make resurrection look ridiculous.
Jesus said their error came from not knowing the scriptures or God’s power.

f.g: Go astray, be mistaken.

n: After the resurrection, marriages are not performed. Latter-day Saints understand from modern revelation that marriages must be sealed by God’s authority in this life to continue after it.

f.w: they neither marry, nor are given in marriage

n: Jesus answered from Moses — the scripture they accepted. At the burning bush God said, “I am the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob” — present tense, long after they had died.

f.w: in the bush God spake unto him

n: God is the God of the living. Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob still live to him. The Sadducees were badly mistaken.
A scribe who had heard the debate and was impressed asked sincerely: which commandment is the most important?
Jesus quoted the Shema, Israel’s daily confession of faith: “Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God is one Lord.”

f.g: Hebrew Shema, “hear,” the first word of this central Jewish prayer.

n: Love God with everything you are — heart, soul, mind, and strength. This is the first commandment.

f.w: thou shalt love the Lord thy God

n: The second is like it: love your neighbor as yourself. No commandments are greater than these two.
The scribe agreed warmly: you’re right, Teacher. There is one God and no other.
He added that loving God and neighbor is worth more than all burnt offerings and sacrifices — echoing the prophets.

f.w: more than all whole burnt offerings

n: Jesus saw the man answered wisely and told him he was not far from God’s kingdom. After that, no one dared ask him more trick questions.

f.g: Wisely, thoughtfully.
Dared.

n: Now Jesus asked a question while teaching in the temple: how can the scribes say the Messiah is merely David’s son?
David, inspired, wrote: “The LORD said to my Lord, sit at my right hand.” David called the Messiah “my Lord.”

f.w: The LORD said to my Lord

f.g: A picture of total victory — enemies under one’s feet.

n: If David calls him Lord, how can he be only David’s descendant? The Messiah is both David’s son and David’s Lord — human and divine. The ordinary people loved listening to him.
Jesus warned against the scribes who loved flowing robes and respectful greetings in public.

f.g: Formal, honoring greetings.

n: They loved the best seats in synagogues and the places of honor at banquets.

f.g: The most honored places at the table.

n: They took advantage of vulnerable widows while putting on long prayers for show. Their judgment will be heavier because they used religion to exploit.

f.g: Possibly by mismanaging estates entrusted to them or exploiting widows’ generosity.
Condemnation, judgment.

n: Jesus sat across from the temple treasury, where offering boxes stood, and watched people give. Many wealthy people gave large amounts.

f.g: Trumpet-shaped offering chests in the Court of the Women.

n: A poor widow put in two tiny copper coins — the smallest money in circulation.

f.g: Greek lepta, the smallest copper coins.
A quadrans, a tiny Roman coin — a fraction of a day’s wage.

n: Jesus called his disciples and said she had given more than all the others.

The rich gave from their surplus; she gave everything she had to live on. God measures gifts by the heart and the sacrifice, not the amount. She contrasts sharply with the scribes who “devour widows’ houses.”

f.g: Out of her poverty.
